prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: Python: numeric type operations (language en).
Grid: 3 columns × 17 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Operation" · longest unbreakable unit 91px · widest one-line content 107px
  col 2: header "Result" · longest unbreakable unit 77px · widest one-line content 504px
  col 3: header "Full documentation" · longest unbreakable unit 109px · widest one-line content 138px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 720px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). The column widths must sum to at most 719px: the table must fit; no horizontal scrolling.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Your understanding: {"purpose":"Provide a compact reference for Python numeric operations, their results, and links to fuller documentation where available.","tasks":["Find an operator or function in the first column and read its result across the row.","Compare related operations, such as division and floor division, or pow(x, y) and x ** y.","Scan the table sequentially to discover available operations.","Locate a documentation link for an operation when one is provided."],"relations":["Each row connects an operation to its result and, for some functions, a documentation link.","The first and last columns contain related code identifiers, while the middle column explains their behavior.","Empty documentation cells are meaningful absences and should remain easy to distinguish from links."],"roles":["The header names the three fields; the body contains one operation per row.","The operation column is the primary lookup index.","The result column carries the explanatory text and has the greatest variation in length.","The documentation column is a secondary navigation aid."],"keep_whole":["Code identifiers and function names such as c.conjugate(), complex() and divmod().","Operators and their operands where practical, especially x // y and x ** y.","The expressions inside function calls where practical."],"may_wrap":["Result descriptions may wrap at word boundaries, especially the long complex-number description.","The Full documentation header may wrap between its two words.","A long function call may wrap at a natural separator if space is constrained."],"same_scale":["All operation entries should read as one consistent lookup column.","Result descriptions should share a consistent text measure; occasional taller rows are acceptable.","Documentation links should remain visually comparable across rows."],"h_vs_v":"The table must fit the viewport, so the longest result cannot remain on one line while preserving useful space for the other columns. Giving the result more width limits row growth; narrower result text saves horizontal space for a more generous lookup or documentation column but makes sequential scanning taller."}

Look at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design: what works, what is visually wrong, and the cause (which width). Then either propose up to 3 improved designs (refine the most promising, fix what you saw, or try an important unexplored idea) or, if further changes would not bring a meaningful improvement, set "done": true. Do not resubmit near-identical widths.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"best":["your best design name(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"change":"what and why"}]}
